## Introduction “The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.” — John Tukey Data visualization is a critical step in data analysis, both to explore your data and to communicate your findings: plots can reveal patterns and trends that are hard to see in raw data. In this lecture, you will learn how to create informative, publication-ready plots with the [_ggplot2_](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) package. _ggplot2_ is based on the **"Grammar of Graphics"**, a set of rules to describe plots, and creates plots **layer by layer**: you start with your data, and then add layers that e.g. represent the data points ("geoms"), change the colors, or add axis labels. Because you can add as many layers as you want, plots are fully customizable. ### Overview & learning goals In this lecture, you will learn: - Basic syntax of the `ggplot()` function, including aesthetic mappings with `aes()` - How to create scatter plots, bar graphs, and box plots with `geom_point()`, `geom_col()`, `geom_bar()`, and `geom_boxplot()` - How to add titles and labels with `labs()`, and apply themes like `theme_bw()` - How to facet plots using `facet_wrap()` and `facet_grid()` - How to set figure captions and sizes with Quarto chunk options - How to export plots in different formats ## Setting up ### A new Quarto document Create a new Quarto document and save it as `week13b.qmd` in your `week13` folder ([Creating a Quarto document](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document)), and add a YAML header. ### Loading packages For this lecture, we will use two packages: the _tidyverse_, which includes _ggplot2_, and _palmerpenguins_, which contains a data set with penguin measurements. You installed both in week 12, so you only need to load them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ✔ dplyr 1.2.1 ✔ readr 2.2.0 ✔ forcats 1.0.1 ✔ stringr 1.6.0 ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3 ✔ tibble 3.3.1 ✔ lubridate 1.9.5 ✔ tidyr 1.3.2 ✔ purrr 1.2.2 ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ℹ Use the conflicted package () to force all conflicts to become errors ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} library(palmerpenguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output Attaching package: 'palmerpenguins' The following objects are masked from 'package:datasets': penguins, penguins_raw ``` ::: ::: Let's take a look at the `penguins` data set and its structure: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} View(penguins) str(penguins) ``` ::: ::: callout-warning #### Two `penguins` data sets Since version 4.5, R itself also comes with a `penguins` data set, but with shorter column names (e.g. `bill_len` instead of `bill_length_mm`). Make sure to load the _palmerpenguins_ package as above, so that `penguins` refers to that package's version, which we use in this lecture. ::: ::: {.callout-note} #### The penguins data set This data set contains body measurements of penguins of 3 species collected on 3 islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. It has 344 observations (rows) and 8 variables (columns): - species (factor): Species of penguin (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) - island (factor): Island where the penguin was found (Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen) - bill_length_mm (num): Length of the penguin's bill in millimeters - bill_depth_mm (num): Depth of the penguin's bill in millimeters - flipper_length_mm (int): Length of the penguin's flipper in millimeters - body_mass_g (int): Body mass of the penguin in grams - sex (factor): Sex of penguins - year (int): Year of data collection To see which data sets are available in a specific R package, use e.g. `data(package = "palmerpenguins")`. ::: ## Creating a ggplot To create a plot with the _ggplot2_ package, you start with the function `ggplot()` (note: the package is called _ggplot2_, but the function `ggplot()`). A basic ggplot has three components: 1. **Data**: the data frame with the variables to be plotted --- here, the `penguins` data set. 2. **Aesthetic mappings**: how variables in the data are mapped to visual properties of the plot, such as the x and y axes, colors, shapes, and sizes. 3. **Geometries ("geoms")**: layers that represent the data, e.g. as points (scatter plot), bars, or boxes. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} The [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf) gives an overview of the many types of plots you can create with _ggplot2_. ::: #### Data The first argument of `ggplot()` is your data frame, which you can provide inside the function, or by piping it into the function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Two ways of passing the data frame to ggplot(): ggplot(data = penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # We will use this style throughout the lecture: penguins |> ggplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-2.png){width=672} ::: ::: We get a blank plot because we haven't told `ggplot()` _what_ to plot yet: we only specified the data frame. Next, we will map variables to the x and y axes with the aesthetics function `aes()`. ### Aesthetic mappings (aes) **Aesthetic mappings** define how variables in the data are mapped to visual properties of the plot. The `x` and `y` arguments of the `aes()` function define the variables to be plotted on the x-axis and y-axis, respectively. Let's say we want to create a scatter plot with `bill_length_mm` on the x-axis and `bill_depth_mm` on the y-axis: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Now the axes are there, but there are still no data points, because we haven't told `ggplot()` _how_ to represent the data. For that, we need to add a geometry (**geom**) layer, such as `geom_point()` for a scatter plot, `geom_bar()` for a bar graph, or `geom_boxplot()` for a box plot. Because both of our variables are continuous, a scatter plot is a good choice: we'll add a `geom_point()` layer using the `+` operator. ## Scatter plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Finally, we can see the scatter plot! Next, let's add a third variable to the plot by coloring the points by penguin `species`. To do so, we map the `species` variable to `color` inside the `aes()` function. When a categorical variable is mapped to color, _ggplot2_ automatically assigns a color to each category, and adds a legend that shows which color corresponds to which category: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Now, each point is colored by the species of the penguin. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise-1: - What do you think will happen if you keep `color = species` outside of `aes()`? There are actually three different ways to do this -- try each one and see what happens: a. `ggplot(aes(x = ..., y = ...), color = species)` -- still inside `ggplot()`, but outside `aes()` b. `geom_point(color = species)` -- inside `geom_point()`, outside `aes()` c. `geom_point(color = "red")` -- inside `geom_point()`, outside `aes()`, but with a fixed value instead of a variable
Click for the solution a. Inside `ggplot()` but outside `aes()`, `color = species` is silently ignored, so all points are colored black (the default) and no legend is added: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm), color = species) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning in fortify(data, ...): Arguments in `...` must be used. ✖ Problematic argument: • color = species ℹ Did you misspell an argument name? ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: b. Inside `geom_point()`, outside `aes()`, the same `color = species` instead produces an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(color = species) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` error-r-output Error: ! object 'species' not found ``` ::: ::: c. But with a fixed value instead of a variable name, it works fine (more on this in the next exercise): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(color = "red") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Why does (b) fail while (c) works, given that both are outside `aes()`?** Anything outside `aes()` is treated as a **fixed setting** rather than a mapping, so it must be given a literal value (like `"red"`) that `geom_point()` can use directly to color every point. `species` isn't a variable that exists outside of the `penguins` data frame, so outside of `aes()`, R has no idea what it refers to and throws an error. In (a), by contrast, `ggplot()` simply ignores the `color` argument entirely because it's outside `aes()` and not a recognized argument of `ggplot()` itself, so `color = species` has no effect at all.
- Create a scatter plot with `bill_length_mm` on the x-axis and `bill_depth_mm` on the y-axis. Color the points by `species`, and map `island` to the shape of the points.
Click for the solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes( x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species, shape = island )) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: See the [_ggplot2_ documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html) for other aesthetics that you can map variables to.
::: ### Mapping vs settings Sometimes you want to give all points the same color or size. To **map** a variable to an aesthetic, put it inside `aes()`; to **set** an aesthetic to a fixed value, put it outside `aes()`, like with `geom_point(color = "red")` in the previous exercise. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise-2: What do you think will happen if you put `color = "red"` _inside_ `aes()`? Predict first, then run the code to check: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = "red")) ``` :::
Click for the solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = "red")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The points are not red, but ggplot's default first color (salmon), and a legend appears with a single entry: "red". Inside `aes()`, `"red"` is treated as _data_: a variable with the value "red" for every point, which is mapped to the first color of ggplot's default color palette.
::: ### Global and local mappings In the examples above, we mapped aesthetics like `color = species` inside `ggplot()`, which is the **global level**: these mappings are passed down to all geom layers. Alternatively, each geom layer can have its own aesthetic mappings at the **local level**. To see the difference, let's add a second geom, `geom_smooth()`, which adds a trend line: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Above, we mapped `color = species` at the global level inside `ggplot()`, so both the points and the lines are colored by species, and `geom_smooth()` fits a separate line for each species. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Here, we mapped `color = species` at the local level inside `geom_point()`. Therefore, only the points are colored by species, while `geom_smooth()` fits a single line across all species, in the default color (blue). ### Manually changing the colors So far, we've used ggplot's default colors. To pick the colors yourself, use the `scale_color_manual()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + scale_color_manual(values = c("grey55", "orange", "skyblue")) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The colors are assigned in the order of the species in the legend. Run `colors()` to see the names of all colors that R knows. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} For ready-made color palettes, see the [optional R self-study page](../bonus/r.qmd#color-palettes). ::: ### Adding titles and labels To add a title and change the axis labels, use the `labs()` function, with arguments `title`, `x`, and `y`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + labs( title = "Scatter plot of bill length vs bill depth", x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Adjusting themes You can change the overall look of a plot by applying a pre-defined **theme**. _ggplot2_ has [several of these](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html), such as `theme_minimal()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_bw()`, and `theme_light()`. Let's apply `theme_bw()` to our previous plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + labs( title = "Scatter plot of bill length vs bill depth", x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)" ) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} You can also customize individual theme elements like font sizes and the legend position with the `theme()` function: see the [optional R self-study page](../bonus/r.qmd#customizing-themes). ::: ## Other geoms So far, we've only made scatter plots with `geom_point()`, but there are many other geoms to create different types of plots. ### Bar graphs Bar graphs are commonly used to show a numeric summary, like a mean, or a count, per group. First, let's plot the mean body mass of penguins on each island. To do so, we first compute the means with `group_by()` and `summarize()`, which you learned about on Monday: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Before plotting, compute the mean island_means <- penguins |> group_by(island) |> summarize(mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) # remove missing values ``` ::: Then, we use `geom_col()` to plot these means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} island_means |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = mean_body_mass)) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: To plot the _number of penguins_ per island instead, you can use `geom_bar()` directly on the full data set, which counts the rows for each value of the `x` variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Box plots Box plots show the distribution of a numeric variable for each category of a categorical variable. Let's create a box plot of the distribution of `body_mass_g` on each `island`. This time, we'll save the plot as an object, `box_plot_body_mass_and_island`, so we can reuse it later: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} box_plot_body_mass_and_island <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() box_plot_body_mass_and_island ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise-3: 1. Add the individual data points to the box plot above, using the `geom_jitter()` function.
Click for the solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Note that without `outlier.shape = NA`, the boxplot's outliers would be shown twice: by `geom_boxplot()` _and_ by `geom_jitter()`.
2. Color these points by penguin species.
Click for the solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(aes(color = species)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
::: There are many other geoms, e.g. for histograms and line graphs: see the [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf) for an overview. ## Multi-panel figures: faceting When you map many variables in a single plot, it can get cluttered. An alternative is **faceting**: creating multiple panels ("facets"), one for each value of a categorical variable. There are two faceting functions: - `facet_wrap()` --- Facet by a single categorical variable, with the panels "wrapped" into a rectangular layout. - `facet_grid()` --- Facet by one or two categorical variables, with the panels laid out in a grid of rows and columns. For example, to facet the box plot from above by species: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_wrap(vars(species)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: And to facet by both species (columns) and sex (rows): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() + facet_grid(rows = vars(sex), cols = vars(species)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Figure options in Quarto documents When you render a Quarto document, any plots made in code chunks will be included in the output document. You can control how they are shown with chunk options that start with `fig-`. For example: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| fig-cap: "Body mass of penguins on different islands" #| fig-width: 6 #| fig-height: 4 #| fig-align: center penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ```` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warning-r-output Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_boxplot()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Body mass of penguins on different islands](w13b_data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: - `fig-cap` --- Add a figure caption below the plot - `fig-width` and `fig-height` --- Set the size of the plot (in inches) - `fig-align` --- Align the plot to the `left`, `right`, or `center` ## Exporting plots To save a plot to a file, in formats like PNG, JPEG, or PDF, use the [`ggsave()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html) function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave( filename = "results/boxplot.png", # file path and name (the 'results' dir must exist) plot = box_plot_body_mass_and_island, # what to save width = 18, height = 12, dpi = 300, # dots per inch, i.e. resolution units = "cm" # units for width and height ) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} For plots that you made in the console, you can also click the `Export` button in RStudio's Plots tab (bottom right), but `ggsave()` gives you more control and is reproducible. ::: ## Recap In this lecture, you learned: - The basic syntax of _ggplot2_, which builds plots layer by layer - How to map variables to aesthetics with `aes()`, and set aesthetics to fixed values outside of it - How to make different types of plots with `geom_*()` functions - How to facet plots with `facet_wrap()` and `facet_grid()` - How to set figure captions and sizes with Quarto chunk options, and how to save plots to files with `ggsave()`
